prompt: A company needs to ensure that users can only create virtual machines in the West US and East US regions. This policy must apply to all subscriptions under a management group. What should you configure?

options.text: Azure Policy with the Allowed locations built-in definition, assigned at the management group scope so that every subscription inherits it
Azure RBAC role assignment at the management group level that gives the VM Contributor role only to the users in the two regions
Resource locks on all resource groups in every subscription, with a CanNotDelete lock on groups outside the two regions
Subscription-level budget alerts that email the owners whenever spending rises in a region outside the approved list

explanation:
Azure Policy with the "Allowed locations" built-in policy definition enforces regional restrictions. Applying it at the management group scope ensures all subscriptions inherit the policy. RBAC controls who can perform actions, not where. Resource locks prevent modification/deletion, not location. Budget alerts are for cost management.

Key concept: Azure Policy Overview (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/policy/overview)

prompt: A company has Microsoft 365 users who need access to Azure resources. They want to use existing identities without creating separate Azure AD accounts. The company already has Azure AD Connect synchronizing on-premises AD. What additional configuration is needed?

options.text: Configure Azure AD B2B collaboration, inviting each Microsoft 365 user as a guest so that the identity exists in the Azure tenant
Azure AD B2C with a customer tenant for the users
No additional configuration - Azure AD Connect already handles this
Install a second Azure AD Connect server in staging mode so that Azure resources can use the synchronized identities

explanation:
Microsoft 365 uses Azure AD (now Entra ID) for identity. If Azure AD Connect is already synchronizing on-premises AD to Azure AD, those identities are available for both M365 and Azure resources. Users authenticate with the same credentials for both. B2B is for external users. B2C is for customer-facing apps. Second AD Connect isn't needed.

Key concept: Azure AD Connect (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/hybrid/whatis-azure-ad-connect)

prompt: A company needs to delegate the ability to create and manage virtual machines to a team without giving them access to modify networking or storage resources. Which built-in RBAC role should be assigned?

options.text: Owner
Contributor
Virtual Machine Administrator Login
Virtual Machine Contributor

explanation:
Virtual Machine Contributor role allows managing VMs and their attached resources but not the underlying virtual network or storage account permissions. Contributor has broader permissions including networking and storage. Owner includes full access plus role assignment. VM Administrator Login is for VM login access, not management.

Key concept: Azure Built-in Roles (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles)

prompt: An organization wants to prevent accidental deletion of a production resource group containing critical databases. Users should still be able to modify resources within the group. What should you implement?

options.text: Read-only lock on the resource group
Delete lock on the resource group, which blocks deletion but still allows edits
Azure Policy with the Audit effect on delete operations
Remove Contributor role from users

explanation:
A Delete lock prevents deletion of the resource group and its resources while allowing modifications. Read-only lock would prevent modifications. Azure Policy with Audit only reports and does not block deletion. Removing Contributor would prevent modifications.

Key concept: Azure Resource Locks (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/management/lock-resources)

prompt: A company needs to track all changes made to Azure resources for compliance auditing. They need to know who made what change and when. What should they configure?

options.text: Resource health alerts
Azure Activity Log with export to Log Analytics
Azure Advisor recommendations, which list reliability, security, and cost improvements for the deployed resources
Azure Monitor Metrics, which store numeric performance data for each resource and can be charted over time

explanation:
Activity Log captures control plane operations (who did what, when) for Azure resources. Exporting to Log Analytics enables querying historical data beyond the 90-day retention and creating compliance reports. Metrics are for performance data. Resource health tracks availability. Advisor provides recommendations, not audit trails.

Key concept: Azure Activity Log (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/essentials/activity-log)

prompt: A company with multiple subscriptions wants to organize them into a hierarchy for policy and access management. Development subscriptions should inherit different policies than production. What should they create?

options.text: Multiple Azure AD tenants, one for development and one for production, with each subscription linked to its own tenant
Management groups with production and development groups
Resource groups in each subscription, named for development and production, with policies assigned to each group
Azure Blueprints assigned to each subscription, with a different blueprint definition for development and production

explanation:
Management groups enable hierarchical organization of subscriptions. Policies and RBAC applied to a management group are inherited by all subscriptions within it. Creating separate groups for dev and prod allows different policies. Multiple tenants complicate identity management. Resource groups are within subscriptions, not for organizing subscriptions. Blueprints are for environment templates.

Key concept: Management Groups (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/management-groups/overview)

prompt: A company needs to provision consistent environments for new projects, including virtual networks and VMs. They want to store the template in Azure as a versioned resource, control who can deploy it with Azure RBAC, and deploy it to many subscriptions. What should they use?

options.text: A Bicep file kept on an administrator's laptop and emailed to teams whenever they ask for it
Template specs, which store a versioned ARM template as an Azure resource that is shared and deployed with RBAC
Azure Resource Graph queries that read the resources in each subscription
Azure Policy initiatives, which group policy definitions for assignment

explanation:
Template specs store an ARM template or Bicep file as an Azure resource with versions. Access is controlled with Azure RBAC, and users can deploy it to any subscription scope. Azure Blueprints used to package this, but it is being retired (January 31, 2027) in favor of template specs and Deployment Stacks. A local file has no versioning or access control. Resource Graph only queries resources. Initiatives group policies only.

Key concept: Template specs (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/bicep/template-specs)

prompt: A company needs to store files that will be accessed by multiple Azure VMs across different regions. The files are accessed frequently and must support SMB protocol. What storage solution should they use?

options.text: Azure Blob Storage with the hot tier, mounted on each VM through the NFS 3.0 endpoint of the storage account
Azure Queue Storage, with a queue per VM that holds the file contents for the other machines to read
Azure Files with an SMB share on the Premium tier
Azure Disk Storage with shared disks, attached to each of the VMs across the regions through a cluster

explanation:
Azure Files provides fully managed SMB file shares accessible by multiple VMs. Premium tier offers high performance for frequent access, and VMs in other regions can mount the share over the network. Blob Storage doesn't support SMB natively. Disk Storage attaches to single VMs. Queue Storage is for messaging.

Key concept: Azure Files (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/files/storage-files-introduction)

prompt: An application stores images in Azure Blob Storage. Images are frequently accessed for the first 30 days, rarely accessed for the next 90 days, and then must be retained for 7 years for compliance. How should you configure storage to minimize cost?

options.text: Configure lifecycle management rules: hot → cool after 30 days → archive after 120 days
Use the hot tier for all blobs and archive them by hand after 120 days
Use premium block blob storage for all blobs, which offers the lowest latency for the images in the first 30 days
Store all blobs in the archive tier from the start, for the lowest price

explanation:
Lifecycle management automatically transitions blobs between tiers based on age. Hot for frequent access (first 30 days), cool for infrequent (30-120 days), archive for long-term retention (7 years). This optimizes cost automatically. Manual archiving requires ongoing effort. Premium is expensive for archival. Archive from start would require rehydration for initial frequent access.

Key concept: Blob Lifecycle Management (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/lifecycle-management-overview)

prompt: A storage account contains sensitive data. The security team requires that data is encrypted with a key managed in Azure Key Vault, and the key must be rotated annually. What should you configure?

options.text: Microsoft-managed keys (default encryption), which Microsoft rotates on its own schedule with no key in your Key Vault
Client-side encryption, where the app encrypts each blob before upload
Customer-managed keys (CMK) in Key Vault, with an automatic annual key rotation policy
Infrastructure encryption, which adds a second layer of platform encryption

explanation:
Customer-managed keys allow you to use your own keys stored in Key Vault. Key Vault supports automatic key rotation policies. Storage accounts can be configured to use CMK for encryption at rest. Microsoft-managed doesn't provide customer control over rotation. Client-side requires application changes. Infrastructure encryption is a secondary encryption layer, not key management.

Key concept: Customer-Managed Keys (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/customer-managed-keys-overview)

prompt: A company needs to provide time-limited access to a specific blob for a partner organization. The partner should only be able to download the file for the next 24 hours without requiring Azure AD credentials.

options.text: Make the blob container public for 24 hours, then set it back to private
Allow anonymous read access on the storage account, then disable it later
Create an Azure AD guest user for the partner, assign the Storage Blob Data Reader role, and delete the guest later
Generate a shared access signature (SAS) with 24-hour expiry and read permissions

explanation:
SAS provides time-limited, permission-scoped access to blobs without requiring authentication setup. You can specify expiry (24 hours) and permissions (read only). Public access would expose the blob to everyone. Guest users require Azure AD setup for external organization.

Key concept: Shared Access Signatures (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-sas-overview)

prompt: A storage account is configured with network rules to allow access only from a specific virtual network. An Azure Function in a different virtual network needs to access the storage account. What should you configure?

options.text: Add the Function's private IP address range to the storage account firewall as an allowed IP rule
Disable the firewall on the storage account so the Function can reach it from any network, then enable it again later
Use managed identity authentication for the Function, with a role assignment on the storage account
Configure a private endpoint for the storage account and VNet peering between the networks

explanation:
Private endpoints provide private IP access to storage accounts over VNet peering or VPN. The Function's VNet can peer with the endpoint's VNet, enabling private access while maintaining firewall restrictions. A private IP range cannot be used in a storage firewall IP rule. Disabling firewall removes security. Managed identity is for authentication, not network access.

Key concept: Private Endpoints (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/private-link/private-endpoint-overview)

prompt: A company must ensure that deleted blobs can be recovered for 30 days. They also need to recover from accidental overwrites. What should they enable?

options.text: Soft delete for containers only, with 30-day retention
A CanNotDelete lock on the storage account, which blocks anyone from deleting or overwriting blobs
Geo-redundant storage, which keeps a copy of every blob in the paired region for recovery
Soft delete, blob versioning, and point-in-time restore together

explanation:
Soft delete keeps deleted blobs for the 30-day retention period. Versioning keeps previous versions when blobs are overwritten. Point-in-time restore rolls block blobs back to an earlier state and requires soft delete and versioning to be on. Container-only soft delete does not cover blobs. A lock does not stop data-plane deletes or overwrites. Geo-redundancy replicates deletions and overwrites to the second region.

Key concept: Data Protection Overview (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/data-protection-overview)

prompt: A company needs to deploy a web application that must survive a data center failure within a region. The application uses IaaS virtual machines. What should you configure?

options.text: Deploy VMs across multiple availability zones with a load balancer
Copy the VMs into multiple resource groups in the region
Use a Virtual Machine Scale Set with a single instance
Deploy VMs in a single availability zone, with a Standard load balancer and managed disks that use ZRS

explanation:
Availability zones are physically separate data centers within a region. Deploying VMs across zones with a zone-redundant load balancer ensures the application survives a single data center failure. Single zone doesn't protect against zone failure. Single-instance VMSS doesn't provide redundancy. Resource groups are logical groupings, not physical separation.

Key concept: Availability Zones (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/reliability/availability-zones-overview)

prompt: A web application experiences variable traffic with peaks on weekends. You want to automatically scale the number of VM instances between 2 and 10 based on CPU utilization. What should you deploy?

options.text: Virtual Machine Scale Set with autoscale rules
Azure Batch
Virtual machines with Azure Automation runbooks that add or remove machines by hand
Load balancer with health probes that take unhealthy VMs out of rotation

explanation:
Virtual Machine Scale Sets (VMSS) provide automatic scaling based on metrics like CPU. Autoscale rules define thresholds (e.g., scale out at 70% CPU, scale in at 30%) and instance limits (min 2, max 10). Automation runbooks require custom logic. Load balancer distributes traffic but doesn't scale. Azure Batch is for batch processing jobs.

Key concept: VMSS Autoscale (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machine-scale-sets/virtual-machine-scale-sets-autoscale-overview)

prompt: A development team needs to run containers without managing infrastructure. The containers run batch jobs that complete in a few minutes and don't need to be always running. What service should they use?

options.text: Azure App Service, with a WebJob that runs each batch task and scales out when the job queue grows
Azure Container Instances (ACI)
Virtual Machines with Docker installed, started by a schedule before each job and shut down when it ends
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), with a Kubernetes Job for each batch run on a node pool that scales to zero

explanation:
Azure Container Instances provide serverless container execution without managing infrastructure. They're ideal for batch jobs and short-lived workloads with per-second billing. AKS requires cluster management. App Service is for web apps, not batch jobs. VMs require infrastructure management.

Key concept: Azure Container Instances (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-instances/container-instances-overview)

prompt: A company is migrating Windows Server VMs from on-premises to Azure. They want to bring their existing Windows Server licenses with Software Assurance to reduce costs. How should they configure the VMs?

options.text: Use Dev/Test subscription
Enable Azure Hybrid Benefit on the VMs
Select Windows Server license during VM creation
Request a discount from Microsoft

explanation:
Azure Hybrid Benefit allows using existing Windows Server licenses with Software Assurance on Azure VMs, reducing the cost to base compute rate. It can be enabled during or after VM creation. Regular license selection includes Windows license cost. Dev/Test is for development workloads. Discounts are enterprise agreements, not license mobility.

Key concept: Azure Hybrid Benefit (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/windows/hybrid-use-benefit-licensing)

prompt: A VM is running low on disk space. The OS disk is 128GB and needs to be increased to 256GB. What steps are required?

options.text: Add a data disk instead, then move the application files to it and leave the 128GB OS disk as it is today
Create a new 256GB disk, copy the data to it, and swap it in as the OS disk
Stop (deallocate) the VM, resize the OS disk, start the VM, then extend the partition in the OS
Resize the disk while the VM is running, and the OS then uses the new space automatically with no extra steps

explanation:
OS disk resizing requires the VM to be stopped (deallocated). After Azure resizes the disk, the VM is started and the partition must be extended within the OS to use the new space. Only eligible data disks can be expanded without deallocating the VM, so an OS disk cannot be resized while running. The partition must also be extended inside the OS. Creating a new disk is more complex. Data disk doesn't solve OS disk space issues.

Key concept: Expand virtual hard disks attached to a Windows VM (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/windows/expand-disks)

prompt: A company wants to deploy a web application that automatically scales, supports deployment slots for zero-downtime deployments, and doesn't require managing VMs. The application is a .NET Core app. What should they use?

options.text: Azure Container Instances
Virtual Machine Scale Set
Azure Batch
Azure App Service

explanation:
App Service is a PaaS offering for web apps with built-in autoscaling, deployment slots for staging/swapping, and no VM management. It supports .NET Core natively. VMSS requires managing VMs. ACI is for containers without deployment slots. Batch runs large parallel compute jobs, not web apps.

Key concept: Azure App Service (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/app-service/overview)

prompt: A Windows VM in Azure cannot be accessed via RDP. The VM shows as running in the portal. What should you check first?

options.text: Boot diagnostics and Network Security Group rules
Check the Azure status page for outages in the region, and wait for the incident to be resolved before any change
Increase the VM size to give the machine more CPU and memory, in case the RDP service is starved of resources
Recreate the VM from the last backup

explanation:
Boot diagnostics show console screenshots to identify OS-level issues. NSG rules might be blocking RDP (port 3389). These are the most common causes for RDP connectivity issues. Increasing size is unlikely to help. Recreating is drastic without diagnosis. Azure status should be checked but is less likely for single VM issues.

Key concept: Troubleshoot RDP (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/azure/virtual-machines/troubleshoot-rdp-connection)

prompt: A company needs to run GPU-accelerated machine learning training jobs on Azure. Jobs run for several hours and cost optimization is important. What VM configuration should they use?

options.text: NC-series VMs with Spot pricing
Fsv2-series VMs
Standard D-series VMs
B-series burstable VMs

explanation:
NC-series VMs have NVIDIA GPUs for ML/AI workloads. Spot pricing provides significant discounts (up to 90%) for interruptible workloads. ML training jobs can often checkpoint and resume, making them suitable for Spot. D-series lack GPUs. B-series are for variable workloads, not sustained compute. Fsv2 are compute-optimized but lack GPUs.

Key concept: GPU VMs (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/sizes-gpu)

prompt: A company wants to ensure their VMs are backed up with daily backups retained for 30 days and weekly backups retained for 1 year. What should they configure?

options.text: Azure Site Recovery, which replicates the VMs to a second region and holds recovery points for 30 days
Manual snapshots taken by Azure Automation runbooks each day and deleted after 30 days
Azure Backup, using a Recovery Services vault policy that keeps daily points for 30 days and weekly points for 1 year
Storage account replication to a second region, which keeps a copy of the VM disks that can be restored

explanation:
Azure Backup policies define backup frequency and retention. You can configure daily backups with 30-day retention and weekly backups with 52-week (1 year) retention. Site Recovery is for disaster recovery replication, not backup. Manual snapshots are complex to manage. Storage replication doesn't provide point-in-time recovery.

Key concept: Azure Backup Policies (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/backup/backup-azure-vm-backup-faq)

prompt: A company has two virtual networks in the same region that need to communicate. They want low latency and private IP connectivity. What should they configure?

options.text: Application Gateway
ExpressRoute
VPN Gateway connections
VNet peering between the two virtual networks

explanation:
VNet peering provides low-latency, high-bandwidth connectivity between VNets using the Azure backbone network. Traffic stays private with no gateway required for same-region peering. VPN Gateway adds latency and is for different connectivity scenarios. ExpressRoute is for on-premises connectivity. Application Gateway is for web traffic load balancing.

Key concept: VNet Peering (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-peering-overview)

prompt: A company's Azure VMs need to access Azure Storage privately without traffic going over the internet. They want to keep the storage account firewall enabled while allowing VNet access. What should they configure?

options.text: Disable storage firewall
VPN Gateway
A NAT gateway on the subnet
Service Endpoints for storage on the VNet subnet

explanation:
Service Endpoints extend VNet identity to Azure services, allowing traffic to route privately over the Azure backbone while storage firewall allows the VNet. This is simpler than Private Endpoints for same-region access. A NAT gateway still reaches storage over its public endpoint. VPN is for different networks. Disabling firewall removes security.

Key concept: Service Endpoints (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-service-endpoints-overview)

prompt: A company has a subnet with VMs that should not be accessible from other subnets in the same VNet. Only specific management ports should be allowed from a management subnet. What should you configure?

options.text: A separate VNet for the VMs, peered with the management VNet, with all ports allowed across the peering
Application Security Groups, which group the VMs for use in rules
Azure Firewall deployed in the same subnet as the VMs
Network Security Group on the subnet with deny rules and specific allow rules

explanation:
NSGs can be applied to subnets to control traffic between subnets in the same VNet. Default rules allow VNet-to-VNet traffic, but explicit deny rules can block it with specific allows for management ports. Azure Firewall needs its own dedicated subnet and cannot sit in the VMs' subnet. A separate VNet with open peering still allows all ports. ASGs are for grouping VMs but work with NSGs, not instead of them.

Key concept: Network Security Groups (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/network-security-groups-overview)

prompt: A company wants to route all traffic from their VNet through a network virtual appliance (NVA) for inspection before going to the internet. What should they configure?

options.text: An Azure DNS private zone that resolves internet names to the NVA's address
VNet peering with the NVA's VNet, so the traffic from the VMs is sent to the NVA before it reaches the internet
Service Endpoints on each subnet, so that internet-bound traffic leaves through the Azure backbone and the NVA
User Defined Routes (UDR) with next hop to the NVA

explanation:
User Defined Routes override Azure's default routing. A UDR with 0.0.0.0/0 destination and NVA as next hop forces all internet-bound traffic through the NVA. Service Endpoints are for Azure services. VNet peering doesn't affect routing to internet. A private DNS zone changes name resolution, not the path packets take.

Key concept: User Defined Routes (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-networks-udr-overview)

prompt: A company wants to receive email alerts when their VM CPU exceeds 80% for more than 5 minutes. What should they configure?

options.text: Azure Monitor alert rule with metric condition and email action group
Log Analytics query
Azure Advisor
Azure Service Health

explanation:
Azure Monitor alert rules can trigger on metric conditions (CPU > 80%, aggregation over 5 minutes). Action groups define notification methods (email, SMS, webhook). Advisor provides recommendations, not alerts. Log Analytics is for log queries, not direct metric alerting. Service Health is for Azure service issues.

Key concept: Azure Monitor Alerts (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/alerts/alerts-overview)

prompt: A company needs to analyze logs from multiple Azure resources including VMs, App Services, and Azure SQL. They want to write queries across all logs and create dashboards. What should they configure?

options.text: Use Azure Monitor Metrics, which store numeric time series for each resource and can be charted on a dashboard
Use the Activity Log only, which records control plane operations for each of the subscriptions
Send all logs to a Log Analytics workspace and use KQL queries
Enable diagnostic settings without a destination, so that the logs are generated and held by each resource

explanation:
Log Analytics workspace centralizes logs from multiple sources. Kusto Query Language (KQL) enables cross-resource analysis. Dashboards can be created from query results. Metrics are for numeric time-series, not log analysis. Diagnostic settings need a destination to be useful. Activity Log is limited to control plane operations.

Key concept: Log Analytics (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/logs/log-analytics-overview)

prompt: A company needs to visualize the performance of their entire Azure environment in a single view including VM health, network topology, and application dependencies. What should they use?

options.text: Cost Management dashboard, which charts spending by tag
The Azure Portal resource list, filtered by subscription
Azure Monitor Workbooks with VM Insights and its dependency map view
Resource Graph Explorer, which runs Kusto queries over resource properties across the subscriptions

explanation:
Azure Monitor Workbooks provide customizable dashboards. VM Insights includes performance monitoring and dependency mapping. Network topology visualization shows connections. Together they provide comprehensive environment visibility. Resource list is basic. Resource Graph is for querying resources, not monitoring. Cost Management is for costs.

Key concept: VM Insights (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/vm/vminsights-overview)

prompt: A critical application runs on Azure. The team needs to be notified of Azure service issues that might affect their resources before they see impact. What should they configure?

options.text: Resource health checks
Third-party monitoring
Manual Azure status page monitoring
Azure Service Health alerts for their subscriptions and regions

explanation:
Azure Service Health provides personalized alerts for Azure service issues affecting your specific resources and regions. You can configure alerts to notify via email/SMS/webhook for service issues, planned maintenance, and health advisories. Resource health shows current state, not proactive alerts. Manual monitoring isn't scalable.

Key concept: Azure Service Health (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/service-health/overview)

prompt: A company has deployed resources but wants to ensure they follow Azure best practices for high availability, security, performance, and cost. What tool should they use?

options.text: Azure Blueprints
Azure Advisor recommendations
Microsoft Defender for Cloud with its secure score
Azure Policy

explanation:
Azure Advisor analyzes deployed resources and provides recommendations across reliability, security, performance, cost, and operational excellence. It's a free service that identifies improvements. Policy enforces standards. Blueprints are for environment templates. Security Center (now Defender for Cloud) focuses on security only.

Key concept: Azure Advisor (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/advisor/advisor-overview)

prompt: A company needs to diagnose intermittent VM connectivity issues. They need to capture network traffic for analysis. What tool should they use?

options.text: Connection Monitor, which tests connectivity between endpoints over time and reports latency and reachability
IP flow verify, which checks whether a packet to or from the VM is allowed or denied by the NSG rules
Network Watcher packet capture
NSG flow logs

explanation:
Network Watcher packet capture records network traffic to/from a VM for detailed analysis. Captures can be filtered and downloaded for tools like Wireshark. NSG flow logs show allowed/denied flows but not packet details. Connection Monitor monitors connectivity status. IP flow verify checks if traffic is allowed/denied.

Key concept: Packet Capture (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/network-watcher/packet-capture-overview)

prompt: A company wants to ensure they are alerted when their Azure spending is projected to exceed their monthly budget. What should they configure?

options.text: Azure Cost Management budget with forecast alerts
Resource tags for cost tracking
Pricing calculator
Azure Advisor cost recommendations

explanation:
Cost Management budgets allow setting spending thresholds with alert conditions based on actual or forecasted costs. Forecast alerts notify when projected spend will exceed budget. Advisor provides optimization recommendations, not budget alerts. Tags help categorize costs but don't alert. Pricing calculator is for estimation before deployment.

Key concept: Cost Management Budgets (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cost-management-billing/costs/tutorial-acm-create-budgets)
